title: Integrating text with charts, tables and media
blurb: Combine a passage with a table, chart, timeline or transcript, explain why two sources seem to disagree, and see past a sensational headline.
question: A news article says 60 percent of teens in a state got a flu shot. A health department chart for the same state shows 45 percent. A TEAS item asks for the most likely explanation. Is one source simply wrong, or is something else going on?

teach.body: Formally, integrating sources means combining information from a passage with a chart, table, map, timeline, infographic, video transcript or audio summary; checking whether the sources agree; explaining any discrepancy (different dates, samples or definitions); and identifying what each source adds that the other lacks. In plain English: read both, line them up carefully and answer what neither could answer alone.

Passage: In 2023, Riverside County opened free weekend flu shot clinics at three libraries. County officials say the clinics made it easier for working adults to get vaccinated.

Table: Adults in Riverside County with a flu shot
Year | Adults vaccinated | Weekend clinic sites
2021 | 41% | 0
2022 | 43% | 0
2023 | 49% | 3
2024 | 52% | 3

head: Year
Adults vaccinated
Weekend sites
teach.caption: Read the title, column labels and units before any number.
Rates rose 2 points from 2021 to 2022, then 6 points in 2023, the year the clinics opened.

items: Read the visual's title, labels, units, dates and source first.
Find the passage's claim (the clinics helped adults get vaccinated).
Line them up: same place, same group, same time period, same units?
Answer with what both show together: the rate rose faster after the clinics opened in 2023. Neither source alone shows this.

teach.body: Before deciding one source is wrong, check for a mismatch. Different dates: a 2024 article and a 2022 chart. Different samples: teens aged 16 to 19 versus 13 to 17. Different definitions: 'vaccinated' meaning one dose versus fully vaccinated. Different units: per week versus per month. The 60 percent article and 45 percent chart may both be accurate if they measure different groups or years.

teach.text: Integration traps: mixing units or time periods, reading the wrong row or legend, extending a chart beyond its data, and trusting a headline over the numbers. A headline like 'Flu Shots Soar!' may describe a 3-point rise. Check the original data and look for other sources that confirm it.

teach.body: Jordan Ellis, applying to a surgical technology program, sees an article saying 60 percent of the state's teens got a flu shot and a health department chart showing 45 percent. Before calling either wrong, Jordan checks the fine print. The article covers ages 16 to 19 in 2024; the chart covers ages 13 to 17 in 2022. Jordan picks 'The sources describe different age groups and years.'

items: Read a visual's title, labels, units, dates and source before its numbers.
Line up place, group, time period and units across sources.
Apparent conflicts often come from different dates, samples or definitions.
Do not extend a chart beyond its data or trust a headline over the numbers.
The best answer often uses information that only the two sources together provide.

summary: You can now combine a passage with a table, chart, timeline or transcript to answer what neither source shows alone. You can also explain why two sources seem to disagree and check a headline against the data behind it.

A.q:
Read the passage and table.

Passage: Last year, Brookside Hospital added a second triage nurse to its emergency department during evening hours, from 4 p.m. to midnight.

Table: Average ER wait (minutes)
Shift | Before | After
Morning | 38 | 37
Evening | 74 | 45
Overnight | 52 | 51

Which statement is supported by both the passage and the table?
options: Wait times dropped on the shift that got the added nurse.
Wait times dropped by about the same amount on all shifts.
The hospital added triage nurses to all three of its shifts.
Evening waits are now shorter than morning waits.
A.why: The passage says the nurse was added during evening hours, and the table shows the evening wait fell from 74 to 45 minutes while the other shifts barely changed.

whyNot.1: Morning and overnight waits fell by only 1 minute each; the evening dropped 29.
whyNot.2: The passage says one nurse was added, in the evening.
whyNot.3: Evening waits (45 minutes) are still longer than morning waits (37 minutes).

A.q:
Read the passage and chart description.

Passage: The Westfield school district started a free summer reading program in 2022 to help students keep their reading skills over the break.

Chart: Bar graph titled 'Students enrolled in summer reading, Westfield.' 2022: 180 students. 2023: 310 students. 2024: 450 students.

What information does the chart provide that the passage does not?
options: The reason the district created the program
The year the summer reading program began
The number of students enrolled each year
Whether the program improved reading scores
A.why: Only the chart gives enrollment numbers for each year. The passage gives the reason and start year but no numbers.

whyNot.0: The reason (keeping reading skills) comes from the passage.
whyNot.1: The passage states the program started in 2022.
whyNot.3: Neither source reports reading scores; the chart shows enrollment only.

A.q:
Read the two sources.

Source 1 (2024 news article): About 30 percent of adults in Lake County now use a telehealth service.

Source 2 (county health report, data from 2019): About 8 percent of adults in Lake County use a telehealth service.

What is the most likely reason the figures differ?
options: One of the two sources must contain a typing error.
The sources describe two different counties' adults.
The news article is counting teenagers as adults.
The two sources report data from different years.
A.why: The article reflects 2024 and the report uses 2019 data. A five-year gap can easily explain a large change in telehealth use.

whyNot.0: There is a clear, legitimate explanation, so assuming an error is not the best answer.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests the article counted teenagers; this invents a mismatch the text does not show.

B.q:
Read the headline and table.

Headline: 'COUGH SYRUP SALES EXPLODE AS FLU SWEEPS TOWN'

Table: Cough syrup sales at Main Street Pharmacy
Week | Bottles sold
Jan 1-7 | 200
Jan 8-14 | 208
Jan 15-21 | 214

Which statement most accurately describes the data?
options: Sales more than doubled over the three weeks shown.
Sales rose slightly, by about 7 percent, over the weeks.
Sales fell each week as the flu season came to an end.
Sales rose because more people in town caught the flu.
B.why: Sales went from 200 to 214 bottles, a rise of 14, or 7 percent. 'Explode' exaggerates a small, steady increase.

whyNot.0: Doubling would require about 400 bottles; sales reached 214.
whyNot.2: Sales rose each week; they did not fall.
whyNot.3: The table shows sales only; it does not show why they rose, and the cause comes from the headline alone.

B.q:
Read the passage and table.

Passage: Nurse Kim recommends that adults drink about 64 ounces of fluid per day.

Table: Fluid in common drinks
Drink | Amount
Water bottle | 16 oz
Coffee mug | 12 oz
Juice box | 6 oz

Marcus drinks two water bottles and one coffee mug in a day. Based on both sources, how much more fluid does he need to reach Nurse Kim's recommendation?
options: 36 ounces
32 ounces
26 ounces
20 ounces
B.why: Marcus drinks 16 + 16 + 12 = 44 ounces. The recommendation is 64 ounces, so he needs 64 - 44 = 20 more ounces.

whyNot.0: 36 ounces counts one water bottle plus the mug (64 - 28), missing the second bottle.
whyNot.1: 32 ounces counts the two water bottles but forgets the coffee mug.
whyNot.2: 26 ounces uses the juice box (6 oz) instead of the coffee mug (12 oz).

B.q:
Read the transcript excerpt and chart description.

Transcript (podcast, Dr. Ana Ruiz): 'Since our hospital started its walking program for heart patients, readmissions have gone down every year.'

Chart: Line graph titled 'Heart patient readmissions within 30 days, Mercy Hospital.' 2021: 18%. 2022: 15%. 2023: 16%. 2024: 12%. Note below chart: walking program began January 2021.

Which statement is best supported by both sources together?
options: Readmissions fell overall, though they rose slightly in 2023.
Readmissions dropped every single year after the program began.
Readmissions rose overall after the walking program started.
Readmissions at Mercy were higher than at nearby hospitals.
B.why: The chart shows an overall fall from 18 to 12 percent, but 2023 (16 percent) was higher than 2022 (15 percent). The chart corrects the doctor's claim that rates fell every year.

whyNot.1: This repeats the podcast claim, which the chart contradicts for 2023.
whyNot.2: Readmissions fell overall, from 18 to 12 percent.
whyNot.3: Neither source compares Mercy with other hospitals.

C.q:
Read the two sources.

Source 1 (gym newsletter): FitLife Gym has 2,400 members.

Source 2 (city business report): FitLife Gym had 900 people check in at least once a week last month.

Which statement best explains how both figures could be accurate?
options: The newsletter was published several years before the report.
The sources count different things: sign-ups versus weekly users.
The report counted check-ins at a different gym in the same city.
The newsletter counted each member's check-ins as separate people.
C.why: Members are everyone signed up; the report counts only people who checked in at least weekly. Different definitions explain the gap.

whyNot.0: Nothing in the sources suggests a difference in dates.
whyNot.3: Counting visits as people would inflate the check-in report, not the membership figure, and nothing supports it.

C.q: A social media post claims, 'New study: Coffee doubles your risk of heart disease!' It includes no link. A student wants to check the claim. Which step is most useful?
options: Count how many people have shared or liked the post online.
Ask friends whether they believe coffee is bad for the heart.
Find the original study and see whether other sources confirm it.
Look for a different post that makes the same claim about coffee.
C.why: Checking the original study shows what it actually found, and looking for corroboration from other reliable sources confirms or corrects the post's summary.

whyNot.0: Popularity says nothing about accuracy; that would be a bandwagon judgment.
whyNot.1: Friends' opinions are not evidence about the study.
whyNot.3: Another post repeating the claim may copy the same error; it is not the original source.

C.q:
Read the passage and timeline.

Passage: The Greene County Clinic's patient numbers jumped after it began accepting Medicaid, and jumped again when it added Saturday hours.

Timeline: March 2021: clinic opens. September 2021: begins accepting Medicaid. June 2022: adds a pediatric nurse. February 2023: adds Saturday hours.

Based on both sources, when did the clinic's two jumps in patient numbers most likely begin?
options: March 2021 and February 2023
September 2021 and June 2022
June 2022 and February 2023
September 2021 and February 2023
C.why: The passage ties the jumps to accepting Medicaid and adding Saturday hours; the timeline dates those changes to September 2021 and February 2023.

whyNot.0: March 2021 is the clinic's opening, not the start of Medicaid; only the second date is right.
whyNot.1: September 2021 is right, but June 2022 is the pediatric nurse, not Saturday hours.
whyNot.2: February 2023 is right, but June 2022 is the pediatric nurse, not Medicaid.

reteach.title: Think of a map and directions
reteach.question: A friend texts, 'Turn left after the gas station,' and you also have a map app. Why do you need both?

blocks.body: The text tells you the landmark; the map shows distances and street names. Together they get you there. If they seem to disagree, you check before deciding one is wrong: maybe your friend's directions are from before the new road opened (different dates), or the map shows miles while the sign shows kilometers (different units). Integrating sources is the same: line them up, check the fine print, then combine.

blocks.text: A map with no scale and a text from three years ago can both mislead. Always check units and dates before combining.

explain.body: Before using any number, read the title, column or axis labels, units, dates, legend and source. Many wrong answers come from the right number in the wrong row or unit.

head: Feature
Ask
rows: Percent or count? Weeks or months?

test.q: A table is titled 'Clinic visits per month (in hundreds).' The row for May shows 12. How many visits did the clinic have in May?
test.why: The title says values are in hundreds, so 12 means 12 x 100 = 1,200 visits.

whyNot.0: This ignores the unit 'in hundreds' in the title.
whyNot.1: This multiplies by ten instead of one hundred.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by one thousand instead of one hundred.

explain.body: The best answer often needs both sources: the passage explains what changed and why, and the visual gives the numbers and timing. Look for the answer neither could give alone.

test.q:
Read the passage and table.

Passage: In 2023, Pine City opened a new bike-share program downtown.

Table: Average daily bike trips downtown
2022 | 300
2023 | 650
2024 | 700

Which conclusion requires information from BOTH sources?
options: Pine City has a bike-share program downtown.
Daily bike trips downtown rose from 2023 to 2024.
Trips more than doubled when bike-share began.
Downtown averaged 700 daily bike trips in 2024.
test.why: The table shows trips rising from 300 to 650; only the passage says bike-share began in 2023. Linking the jump to the program's first year needs both.

whyNot.0: This comes from the passage alone.
whyNot.1: This comes from the table alone.
whyNot.3: This comes from the table alone.

explain.body: When two sources give different figures, check dates, groups or samples, definitions and units. Two accurate sources can differ because they measure different things.

test.q: A hospital brochure says it has '120 nurses.' A state report says the hospital has '85 full-time registered nurses.' Which is the most likely explanation?
options: The state report is out of date by several years.
The brochure also counts part-time staff and LPNs.
The brochure describes a different hospital's staff.
The state report counts nurses at every state hospital.
test.why: The report counts only full-time registered nurses; a brochure figure of 'nurses' likely includes part-time staff and other nurse types. A different definition explains the gap.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests the report is outdated; the wording points to a definition difference.
whyNot.2: Both sources describe the same hospital.
whyNot.3: The report gives a figure for this hospital, not a state total.

explain.body: Headlines can be sensational, and social media spreads misinformation. Check the original source, compare the headline with the actual data and look for other reliable sources that confirm the claim.

test.q: A headline reads 'Town Water Unsafe!' The water department's report, linked in the article, shows one test site slightly above a safety limit for one day, with all other sites normal. Which statement best describes the headline?
options: It exaggerates a brief problem at a single site.
It accurately reports the department's findings.
It understates a danger the report describes.
It reports results from a different town's water.
test.why: The report shows one site slightly over the limit for one day. 'Town Water Unsafe!' turns a brief, local reading into a town-wide alarm.

whyNot.1: The report does not show the town's water as a whole was unsafe.
whyNot.2: The headline is more alarming than the report, not less.
whyNot.3: The article links the town's own water department report.
